questions.prompt: What are the values of `A` and `B`?
options: Ill-formed: `auto` cannot be the type of a template parameter
questions.explanation: `2 - 1` is the `int` value 1, so `A` names the same specialization twice. For `X<1u>` the placeholder deduces `unsigned int`, and template-argument equivalence requires the same type as well as the same value, so `B` is false. `auto` parameters have been allowed since C++17.

questions.prompt: Which line is ill-formed in C++23?
options: #3, because a null pointer is not an object address
#2, because a pointer argument cannot designate a string literal
questions.explanation: [temp.arg.nontype] forbids a pointer or reference argument from referring to a string literal, a temporary, a `typeid` result or `__func__`, so #2 is ill-formed. Internal linkage has been enough since C++11 and no linkage is needed since C++17, so #1 is fine, and a null pointer value is a valid argument for a pointer parameter. Pass text through a class-type parameter that stores the characters instead.

questions.prompt: In C++20, what does this program print?
options: Nothing: ill-formed because string literals cannot be template arguments
Nothing: ill-formed because `fixed_string` has a user-provided constructor
questions.explanation: The parameter is a placeholder for a deduced class type, so `fixed_string<3>` is deduced from `"ok"` and the class copies the characters. The string-literal ban applies to pointer and reference arguments, not to a class value built from a literal, and user-provided constructors are fine in a structural type. `S` names a template parameter object with static storage duration, so the returned pointer stays valid.

questions.prompt: In C++20, on an implementation with IEEE 754 `double` (such as any x86-64 or arm64 target), what is the value of `same`?
options: Ill-formed: floating-point types cannot be template parameters
questions.explanation: For floating-point arguments, [temp.type] requires the values to be identical, not merely equal under `==`. Positive and negative zero compare equal but are different values, so they give two distinct specializations. Floating-point parameters are allowed since C++20, so the third option describes C++17.

questions.code:
template<double D> struct Scale {};

Scale<1> s;
options: Ill-formed: integral-to-floating conversions are not allowed in a converted constant expression
Well-formed, but `Scale<1>` and `Scale<1.0>` are different types
Ill-formed: floating-point parameters require a floating-point literal with a suffix
questions.explanation: An NTTP argument must be a converted constant expression of the parameter type, and [expr.const] allows only a short list of conversions: non-narrowing integral conversions and promotions, floating-point promotions and exact floating-point conversions, and a few pointer conversions. A floating-integral conversion is not on the list, even though 1 is exactly representable, so the program is ill-formed. GCC and Clang both reject it; write `Scale<1.0>`.

questions.prompt: In C++20, what does this program print?
options: `0`: each function template has its own copy of the argument
Ill-formed: a template parameter is a prvalue and has no address
Undefined behavior: the pointer dangles after `where` returns
questions.explanation: A class-type NTTP names a template parameter object of type `const P` with static storage duration, and no two such objects are template-argument-equivalent, so `f<P{1}>` and `g<P{1}>` both refer to the one object for the value `P{1}`. Taking the address is fine because, unlike a scalar NTTP, the name is an lvalue. The prvalue rule in the second option applies to `template<int N>`, where `&N` is ill-formed.

questions.prompt: Under C++20 rules, which of these class types can be the type of a non-type template parameter?
options: All four, since each is a literal type
questions.explanation: A structural class type must be a literal class whose bases and non-static data members are all public and non-mutable, with structural types. `A` qualifies; its user-provided constexpr constructor does not matter. `B` has a private member, `C` a mutable one, and `D` a private base, so none of them is structural even though all are literal types.

questions.prompt: In which standard versions is `Slot<&arr[1]>` a valid template argument?
options: None: array elements can never be template arguments
questions.explanation: Before C++17 a pointer argument had to be the address of a complete object with linkage, which an array element is not. C++17 accepted any constant expression but still excluded pointers to subobjects. C++20 lifted that exclusion, keeping only the bans on temporaries, string literals, `typeid` results, `__func__` and their subobjects, so the argument is valid from C++20 on.
